title: 6.12 — Logistic Regression for Binary Responses
breadcrumb: Unit VI → Regression and linear models → 6.12 Logistic regression
engineName: Model binary outcomes through log-odds, odds ratios, fitted probabilities and likelihood-based inference.
objectives: Explain why the linear probability model can produce probabilities outside the unit interval and heteroscedastic errors.
Write the logistic regression model using the logit link and convert a linear predictor into a probability.
Interpret logistic coefficients as changes in log-odds and exponentiated coefficients as odds ratios.
Calculate fitted probabilities and marginal effects at specified covariate values.
Describe maximum-likelihood estimation, likelihood-ratio tests and deviance.
Recognise complete separation, classification thresholds and the distinction between probability and odds.

prereq.name: Binary outcomes and conditional probability
prereq.why: Logistic regression models P(Y=1|X) for a binary response.

prereq.name: Odds, logarithms and exponential functions
prereq.why: The logit link is the logarithm of odds, and odds ratios are exponentiated coefficients.

prereq.name: Maximum likelihood estimation
prereq.why: Logistic coefficients are estimated by maximising the Bernoulli likelihood.

traps: The logistic model is linear in the log-odds, not in the probability.
The fitted probability is exp(η)/(1+exp(η)), which always lies strictly between zero and one for finite η.
A coefficient β_j changes log-odds per unit x_j; exp(β_j) is the multiplicative change in odds.
An odds ratio is not a probability ratio or a percentage-point change in probability.
The marginal effect in a simple logit model is βp(1−p), so it depends on the covariate values through p.
Logistic coefficients are estimated by maximum likelihood, not ordinary least squares.
Deviance is based on log-likelihood; a smaller deviance indicates better fit relative to the saturated model.
Complete separation can make ordinary maximum-likelihood estimates diverge.
howto: Write η=X′β, then convert to p=1/(1+exp(−η)). Interpret β as a log-odds coefficient and exp(β) as an odds ratio. For a fitted probability, calculate η first and apply the logistic transformation. For a continuous regressor, the marginal effect is βp(1−p), evaluated at the stated covariate values. Keep probability, odds and odds ratio distinct.

sheet: For binary Y, logistic regression models p(x)=P(Y=1|X=x).
For finite η, fitted probabilities lie strictly between zero and one.
A coefficient β_j changes log-odds by β_j per unit increase in x_j, holding other regressors fixed.
The odds ratio for a one-unit increase in x_j is exp(β_j).
Odds are p/(1−p); odds are not the same as probability.
For a continuous regressor in a simple logit, marginal effect is βp(1−p).
Coefficients are estimated by maximum likelihood under the Bernoulli model.
Deviance compares fitted and saturated log-likelihoods; separation can cause diverging estimates.
cards: No finite ordinary MLE in complete separation
tricks: Convert η to p only after calculating the full linear predictor.
Exponentiate β to get the odds ratio; do not call β itself a percentage change in probability.
At p=0.5, p(1−p)=0.25 and the simple-logit marginal effect is β/4.
For large |η|, p is near zero or one and the marginal effect becomes small.
shortcuts: OR>1 when β>0; OR<1 when β<0.
Probability p and odds p/(1−p) are different scales.
remember: An odds ratio of 2 means the odds double; it does not mean the probability doubles.
The logistic curve is S-shaped and its slope depends on the covariate value.

scenes.title: Refresh binary outcomes, odds and likelihood
scenes.objective: Recover the probability tools needed for logistic regression.
body: A binary response takes values zero and one. The quantity of interest is the conditional probability that the response equals one, given the regressors.
Logistic regression keeps the fitted probability in the unit interval by modelling the log-odds as a linear function of the predictors.

items.ask: What is the odds corresponding to probability p?
refresh: Probability is the chance of success; odds compare the chance of success with the chance of failure.
If p=0.8, the odds are 0.8/0.2=4, meaning four successes per failure in odds terms.
Odds are not themselves probabilities and can exceed one.

items.ask: What is the logit of a probability?
items.recall: log[p/(1−p)], the logarithm of the odds.
refresh: The logit transforms probabilities in (0,1) to the whole real line.
The logistic regression linear predictor η is modelled as the logit of the conditional success probability.
The inverse-logit transformation maps any finite η back into a probability strictly between zero and one.

items.recall: Choose parameter values that maximise the likelihood of the observed data.
refresh: For independent binary observations, the likelihood is the product of Bernoulli probabilities.
The log-likelihood is easier to optimise because it converts the product into a sum.
Logistic regression coefficients are obtained by maximising this log-likelihood, usually numerically.

ask.q: Why is the logit link useful for a binary response?
ask.nudge: It maps an unrestricted linear predictor to a probability between zero and one.

scenes.title: Why not use an unrestricted straight line for probability?
scenes.objective: Build an intuitive reason for the logistic curve.
body: A linear probability model uses E(Y|X)=X′β. It is simple to estimate, but fitted values can be negative or exceed one, and its Bernoulli error variance depends on the probability.
The logistic model instead lets a linear predictor act on the log-odds. The inverse-logit curve is S-shaped and remains between zero and one.
The curve is steepest near p=0.5 and flattens near zero and one, so the same coefficient produces different probability changes at different covariate values.

scenario.title: Keep fitted probabilities valid
body: A bank predicts whether a borrower defaults using income, debt and credit history. A linear probability model can produce a fitted value of 1.12 for a high-risk borrower or −0.08 for a low-risk borrower.
Those numbers cannot be interpreted as probabilities. The logistic model constructs a linear predictor η and converts it through p=1/(1+exp(−η)).
For every finite η the fitted probability lies between zero and one. The effect of a predictor on probability is not constant: it depends on the current fitted probability.
This makes logistic regression a natural model for binary outcomes, while still requiring attention to calibration, specification and the assumptions behind the likelihood.
scenario.q: What guarantees that a finite linear predictor gives a valid probability?
scenario.answer: The inverse-logit transformation maps every finite η into (0,1).

ask.q: Where is the logistic curve steepest?

scenes.title: The logit model and inverse-logit probability
scenes.objective: Write and transform the logistic regression equation.

blocks.body: log[p_i/(1−p_i)]=η_i=β₀+β₁x_{i1}+…+β_kx_{ik}. The linear predictor is a model for log-odds.
Solving for p gives p_i=exp(η_i)/(1+exp(η_i))=1/(1+exp(−η_i)). This is always between zero and one for finite η_i.
Odds are p/(1−p). If p=0.8, odds are 4; if odds are 4, probability is 4/(1+4)=0.8.
The linear probability model has a constant probability slope but may leave [0,1]. Logistic regression has a nonlinear probability curve and a linear log-odds index.

ask.nudge: The odds are exp(0)=1, so success and failure are equally likely.

items.q: What does β_j represent in a logit model?
items.a: The change in log-odds for a one-unit increase in x_j, holding other regressors fixed.

Does an odds ratio of 2 mean the probability doubles?
items.a: No. It means the odds double; the probability change depends on the baseline probability.

items.a: βp(1−p), evaluated at the specified covariate values.

scenes.title: Odds ratios, marginal effects and likelihood
scenes.objective: Interpret coefficients and describe estimation and inference.

blocks.body: A one-unit increase in x_j multiplies the odds by exp(β_j), holding other regressors fixed. If β_j>0, the odds ratio exceeds one; if β_j<0, it is below one.
For a continuous regressor in a simple logit model, ∂p/∂x=βp(1−p). The marginal effect depends on x through p and is largest in magnitude near p=0.5.
The Bernoulli log-likelihood is Σ[y_i log(p_i)+(1−y_i)log(1−p_i)]. The coefficient estimates maximise this function, usually by iterative numerical methods.
Deviance is −2 times the log-likelihood ratio between the fitted model and the saturated model. Likelihood-ratio tests compare nested models using differences in deviance.

ask.q: Why is exp(β) an odds ratio rather than a probability ratio?
ask.nudge: The coefficient is linear in log[p/(1−p)], not in p.

scenes.title: The same odds ratio, different probability changes
scenes.objective: Understand why a logistic marginal effect varies with baseline risk.
body: A coefficient shifts log-odds by a fixed amount. But the probability scale is nonlinear, so the probability change from the same coefficient depends on the starting probability.
Near p=0.5, the logistic curve is steep. Near p=0 or p=1, it is flat. This is why reporting an odds ratio does not fully describe the probability change for every person.

scenario.title: Odds are not probability points
body: A one-unit predictor increase has an odds ratio of 2. For a person whose baseline probability is 0.10, the baseline odds are 0.10/0.90=1/9. Doubling the odds gives 2/9 and a new probability of 2/11≈0.182.
For a person whose baseline probability is 0.50, the baseline odds are 1. Doubling the odds gives odds 2 and a new probability of 2/3≈0.667.
The same odds ratio therefore produces different probability changes: about 8.2 percentage points in the first case and 16.7 points in the second.
An odds ratio is constant for a one-unit change in x in the model, but the marginal effect on probability varies with the covariates.
scenario.q: Why are the probability changes different even though the odds ratio is the same?
scenario.answer: The inverse-logit transformation is nonlinear and depends on the baseline probability.

ask.q: What does a constant odds ratio imply about probability changes?
ask.nudge: It does not imply a constant percentage-point change.

scenes.objective: Interpret a coefficient on both the odds and probability scales.
scenes.problem: A logit model has β=ln(2) for x. At a covariate value where p=0.5, calculate the odds ratio and marginal effect.

steps.why: A one-unit increase doubles the odds.
The probability derivative depends on the current fitted probability.
The local probability slope is about 0.173 per unit x at this point.

ask.q: Would the marginal effect be as large near p=0.02?
ask.nudge: The product p(1−p) is much smaller near zero.

scenes.title: Guided problem: distinguish odds from probability
scenes.objective: Convert between probability and odds without mixing scales.
scenes.problem: A borrower has predicted default probability p=0.8. What are the odds of default, and what probability corresponds to odds of 4?
hints: Odds equal p divided by one minus p.
To reverse odds o into probability, use o/(1+o).
Check that the two calculations are inverse transformations.
scenes.answer: Odds are 0.8/0.2=4; odds of 4 correspond to probability 4/(1+4)=0.8.

solution.why: The denominator in odds is the probability of no default.
The odds are four to one.
This is the inverse odds transformation.
The two transformations recover the original probability.

ask.q: Why can odds exceed one while probabilities cannot?
ask.nudge: Odds divide p by 1−p; the denominator can be smaller than the numerator.

scenes.title: Exam traps: logit, odds and inference
scenes.intro: Mark each statement true or false.

items.claim: The logistic model is linear in the log-odds.
items.why: The logit is the linear predictor X′β.

items.claim: The fitted probability can exceed one for a finite linear predictor.
items.why: The inverse-logit maps finite η into (0,1).

items.claim: exp(β) is the odds ratio for a one-unit increase in x.
items.why: Exponentiating a log-odds change gives the multiplicative odds change.

items.claim: An odds ratio of two means the probability doubles.
items.why: The probability change depends on the baseline probability.

items.claim: Complete separation can prevent finite ordinary maximum-likelihood estimates.
items.why: The likelihood can increase as a coefficient diverges.

scenes.title: Transfer problem: identify separation and deviance
scenes.problem: A predictor perfectly separates all Y=1 observations from all Y=0 observations. What happens to ordinary logistic maximum-likelihood estimates, and what does a likelihood-ratio test compare?
hints: Think about whether a finite coefficient can perfectly separate the outcomes.
Recall the direction of the likelihood as the coefficient grows.
A likelihood-ratio test compares nested models through their log-likelihoods or deviances.
scenes.answer: Complete separation can make ordinary MLE coefficients diverge; a likelihood-ratio test compares the fit of nested models using a deviance difference.

solution.say: Perfect separation means a predictor divides the two outcome classes without overlap.
The likelihood can improve as the separating coefficient grows in magnitude.
A finite ordinary MLE may not exist.
Nested models are compared using twice the log-likelihood difference.

ask.q: What is the key warning from complete separation?
ask.nudge: The coefficient estimate may not converge to a finite value.

scenes.title: Summary: log-odds, odds ratio and probability
scenes.objective: Compress the logistic model into an exam-ready checklist.
body: Logistic regression models log[p/(1−p)]=X′β. The inverse-logit p=1/(1+exp(−X′β)) keeps fitted probabilities between zero and one.

A coefficient is a change in log-odds; exp(β) is the odds ratio. An odds ratio of two doubles odds, not probability. For a continuous regressor, the simple-logit marginal effect is βp(1−p) and varies with the covariate values.
Coefficients are estimated by maximum likelihood. Deviance and likelihood-ratio tests compare model fit. Complete separation can make ordinary maximum-likelihood estimates diverge.

ask.q: What is the safest three-step interpretation of a logit coefficient?
ask.nudge: State the log-odds change, exponentiate for the odds ratio, then calculate a marginal effect if a probability change is requested.

scenes.title: Extension — likelihood and deviance
scenes.objective: Connect logistic estimation to likelihood-based model comparison.

blocks.body: ℓ(β)=Σ[y_i log(p_i)+(1−y_i)log(1−p_i)], with p_i=1/(1+exp(−x_i′β)). The MLE maximises this log-likelihood.
D=−2[ℓ(fitted)−ℓ(saturated)]. A smaller deviance indicates a closer fit to the saturated model.

For nested models, LR=2(ℓ_full−ℓ_restricted)=D_restricted−D_full. Under regularity conditions and the null, it is asymptotically chi-square with degrees of freedom equal to the number of restrictions.

ask.q: What does a deviance difference measure for nested models?
ask.nudge: It is twice the log-likelihood gain from the larger model.
